body.en:
Sorting means arranging data elements in a particular order: ascending (increasing) or descending (decreasing). Example: 45 12 78 34 → 12 34 45 78.

Why sort?

  • Searching becomes much faster (binary search needs sorted data).
  • Reports, merit lists, telephone directories and dictionaries are easier to read.

Types and terms

  • Internal sorting: all data fits in main memory (RAM). E.g. bubble, selection, insertion, quick sort.
  • External sorting: the data is too large for main memory and is kept on disk. E.g. merge sort is used.
  • Stable sort: equal elements keep their original relative order (bubble, insertion, merge, radix). Unstable: selection, quick.
  • In-place sort: needs no (or constant) extra memory (bubble, selection, insertion, quick). Merge and radix need extra memory.
  • Pass: one complete scan over the (unsorted part of the) array.

The efficiency of a sort is measured by the number of comparisons and swaps/moves, written in Big-O notation.

In bubble sort, adjacent elements are compared and swapped if they are in the wrong order. In each pass, the largest remaining element "bubbles up" to its correct position at the end.

Algorithm BUBBLE(A, N)
Step 1: Repeat Step 2 for I = 0 to N-2
Step 2:   Set FLAG = 0
          Repeat for J = 0 to N-2-I
            If A[J] > A[J+1] then
              Swap A[J] and A[J+1]
              Set FLAG = 1
          If FLAG = 0 then go to Step 3
Step 3: Exit

Example: 45 12 78 34 23 56

PassArray after pass (bold = fixed)ComparisonsSwaps
112 45 34 23 56 7854
212 34 23 45 56 7842
312 23 34 45 56 7831
412 23 34 45 56 7820

Total comparisons = 14, swaps = 7. Pass 4 has no swap, so the algorithm stops early (FLAG = 0).

Analysis

  • Passes: at most n − 1. Comparisons: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2.
  • Best case (already sorted, with flag): O(n). Average and worst case: O(n²).
  • Space: O(1), in-place and stable.
  • Advantage: very simple. Disadvantage: slow for large data.

In selection sort, the smallest element of the unsorted part is selected and swapped with the first element of the unsorted part. The sorted part grows from the left by one element in every pass.

Algorithm SELECTION(A, N)
Step 1: Repeat Steps 2-4 for
        I = 0 to N-2
Step 2:   Set MIN = I
Step 3:   Repeat for J = I+1 to N-1
            If A[J] < A[MIN] then
              Set MIN = J
Step 4:   If MIN != I then
            Swap A[I] and A[MIN]
Step 5: Exit

Example: 45 12 78 34 23 56

PassActionArray (bold = sorted part)
1min 12 at [1]; swap with a[0] = 4512 45 78 34 23 56
2min 23 at [4]; swap with a[1] = 4512 23 78 34 45 56
3min 34 at [3]; swap with a[2] = 7812 23 34 78 45 56
4min 45 at [4]; swap with a[3] = 7812 23 34 45 78 56
5min 56 at [5]; swap with a[4] = 7812 23 34 45 56 78

Analysis

  • Comparisons are always n(n − 1)/2 (even for sorted data): best, average and worst case O(n²).
  • Swaps: at most n − 1 (one per pass): useful when writing to memory is costly.
  • Space: O(1), in-place; not stable.

Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time. Each new element (the key) is inserted into its correct position in the already sorted left part, by shifting the larger elements one place to the right. It works the way we arrange playing cards in the hand.

Algorithm INSERTION(A, N)
Step 1: Repeat Steps 2-5 for
        I = 1 to N-1
Step 2:   Set KEY = A[I], J = I - 1
Step 3:   Repeat while J >= 0 and
          A[J] > KEY
            Set A[J+1] = A[J]
            Set J = J - 1
Step 4:   Set A[J+1] = KEY
Step 5: [End of loop]
Step 6: Exit

Example: 45 12 78 34 23 56

PassKeyShiftsPlacedArray (bold = sorted part)
1121at [0]12 45 78 34 23 56
2780at [2]12 45 78 34 23 56
3342at [1]12 34 45 78 23 56
4233at [1]12 23 34 45 78 56
5561at [4]12 23 34 45 56 78

Analysis

  • Best case (sorted data): only one comparison per element, O(n).
  • Average and worst case (reverse order): O(n²).
  • Space O(1), in-place and stable. Very efficient for small or nearly sorted data.

Quick sort is a divide and conquer algorithm (developed by C. A. R. Hoare). One element is chosen as the pivot (here, the first element), and the array is partitioned so that:

  • all elements smaller than (or equal to) the pivot are on its left,
  • all elements greater than the pivot are on its right, and
  • the pivot is at its final sorted position.
Algorithm QUICK(A, LOW, HIGH)
Step 1: If LOW < HIGH then
          K = PARTITION(A, LOW, HIGH)
          QUICK(A, LOW, K-1)
          QUICK(A, K+1, HIGH)
Step 2: Exit

Algorithm PARTITION(A, LOW, HIGH)
Step 1: PIVOT = A[LOW]
        I = LOW + 1, J = HIGH
Step 2: Repeat
          While I <= HIGH and
                A[I] <= PIVOT: I = I+1
          While A[J] > PIVOT: J = J-1
          If I < J then
            Swap A[I] and A[J]
        Until I >= J
Step 3: Swap A[LOW] and A[J]
Step 4: Return J

First partition of 25 57 48 37 12 92 86 33 (pivot 25)

  1. i moves right from 57: 57 > 25, so i stops at index 1. j moves left from 33: 33, 86 and 92 are > 25, so j stops at 12 (index 4). Since i < j, swap 57 and 12 → 25 12 48 37 57 92 86 33.
  2. i continues: 12 ≤ 25, so it moves on and stops at 48 (index 2). j continues: 57, 37 and 48 are > 25, so it stops at 12 (index 1).
  3. Now i > j, so swap the pivot with a[j] → 12 25 48 37 57 92 86 33. 25 is at its final place; everything on its left is ≤ 25 and everything on its right is > 25.

h.en: 5.1.6 Quick Sort: Complete Process and Analysis

body.en:
After partitioning, the left part and the right part are sorted recursively in the same way, until every part has 0 or 1 element.

Example: 25 57 48 37 12 92 86 33

Sub-arrayPivotActionArray
[0..7]25swap 57 and 1225 12 48 37 57 92 86 33
[0..7]25i>j: swap pivot with a[1] → 25 fixed at [1]12 25 48 37 57 92 86 33
[2..7]48swap 57 and 3312 25 48 37 33 92 86 57
[2..7]48i>j: swap pivot with a[4] → 48 fixed at [4]12 25 33 37 48 92 86 57
[2..3]33i>j: swap pivot with a[2] → 33 fixed at [2]12 25 33 37 48 92 86 57
[5..7]92i>j: swap pivot with a[7] → 92 fixed at [7]12 25 33 37 48 57 86 92
[5..6]57i>j: swap pivot with a[5] → 57 fixed at [5]12 25 33 37 48 57 86 92

Analysis

  • Best and average case: O(n log n) (the pivot splits the array into nearly equal halves).
  • Worst case: O(n²), when the array is already sorted or reverse sorted (the pivot is always the smallest or largest).
  • In-place (only the recursion stack, O(log n)); not stable. One of the fastest sorts in practice.
  • Choosing the middle or a random element as the pivot avoids the worst case for sorted data.

Merge sort is also a divide and conquer algorithm:

  1. Divide: split the array into two halves at the middle, M = (L + R) / 2.
  2. Conquer: sort each half recursively, until a part has only one element (which is already sorted).
  3. Combine: merge the two sorted halves into one sorted array.
Algorithm MERGESORT(A, L, R)
Step 1: If L < R then
          M = (L + R) / 2
          MERGESORT(A, L, M)
          MERGESORT(A, M+1, R)
          MERGE(A, L, M, R)
Step 2: Exit

Algorithm MERGE(A, L, M, R)
Step 1: I = L, J = M+1, K = 0
Step 2: While I <= M and J <= R
          If A[I] <= A[J] then
            T[K++] = A[I++]
          Else T[K++] = A[J++]
Step 3: Copy the rest of A[I..M]
        and A[J..R] into T
Step 4: Copy T back into A[L..R]

Example: 38 27 43 3 9 82 10

Divide: [38 27 43 3] and [9 82 10] → [38 27] [43 3] [9 82] [10] → single elements.

LevelMergeResult
2[38] + [27][27 38]
2[43] + [3][3 43]
1[27 38] + [3 43][3 27 38 43]
2[9] + [82][9 82]
1[9 82] + [10][9 10 82]
0[3 27 38 43] + [9 10 82][3 9 10 27 38 43 82]

Analysis

  • Best, average and worst case: always O(n log n) (log n levels, O(n) merging work per level).
  • Needs an extra array: space O(n). Stable.
  • Used for external sorting (large files) and for sorting linked lists.

Radix sort (bucket sort) sorts numbers digit by digit, without comparing elements with each other. It starts from the least significant digit (units) and moves to the most significant digit, using 10 buckets (0 to 9) for decimal numbers.

Algorithm RADIX(A, N)
Step 1: Find MAX; D = number of
        digits in MAX
Step 2: Repeat for P = 1 to D
          a) Empty buckets 0 to 9
          b) For each A[I]: digit =
             P-th digit from right;
             put A[I] in bucket[digit]
          c) Collect buckets 0..9 in
             order back into A
Step 3: Exit

Example: 170 45 75 90 802 24 2 66

The largest number, 802, has 3 digits, so there are 3 passes.

Analysis

  • Time: O(d × n), where d = number of digits. For small d it is effectively linear.
  • Extra space for buckets: O(n + 10). Stable.
  • Works for integers and strings of fixed length; not suitable for real numbers directly.

SortBestAverageWorstExtra spaceStableMethod
BubbleO(n)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)Yesexchange
SelectionO(n²)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)Noselection
InsertionO(n)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)Yesinsertion

MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n log n)O(n)Yesdivide and conquer

Which one to use?

  • Small or nearly sorted data → insertion sort.
  • Large data in memory, fastest on average → quick sort.
  • Guaranteed O(n log n), linked lists, external files → merge sort.
  • Integers with few digits → radix sort.
  • Fewest swaps → selection sort.

Searching is the process of finding whether a given element (the key) is present in a collection and, if so, its position. The search is successful if the key is found, otherwise unsuccessful.

In linear (sequential) search, the key is compared with each element one by one, from the first to the last, until a match is found or the list ends.

Algorithm LINEAR(A, N, KEY)
Step 1: Repeat for I = 0 to N-1
          If A[I] = KEY then
            Write "Found at", I
            and Exit
Step 2: Write "Not found"
Step 3: Exit

Example: search 56 in 34 12 78 23 56 45 9 → compared with 34, 12, 78, 23, 56 → found at index 4 after 5 comparisons.

Analysis

  • Best case: key at the first position, O(1).
  • Worst case: key at the last position or absent, n comparisons, O(n).
  • Average: about n/2 comparisons, O(n).
  • Advantage: simple; works on unsorted data and on linked lists. Disadvantage: slow for large lists.

Binary search works only on a sorted array. The key is compared with the middle element:

  • if equal, the search is successful;
  • if the key is smaller, the search continues in the left half;
  • if the key is larger, the search continues in the right half.

Each comparison removes half of the remaining elements.

Algorithm BINARY(A, N, KEY)
Step 1: Set LOW = 0, HIGH = N-1
Step 2: Repeat while LOW <= HIGH
          MID = (LOW + HIGH) / 2
          If A[MID] = KEY then
            Write "Found at", MID
            and Exit
          Else If KEY < A[MID] then
            HIGH = MID - 1
          Else
            LOW = MID + 1
Step 3: Write "Not found"
Step 4: Exit

Example: search 23 in 5 12 18 23 34 45 56 67 78 89

lowhighmida[mid]Decision
0943423 < 34: high = 3
0311223 > 12: low = 2
2321823 > 18: low = 3
3332323 = 23: found

Found at index 3 in 4 comparisons. (Linear search would also need 4 here, but for 89 binary search needs 4 while linear search needs 10.)

Analysis

  • Best case O(1) (key in the middle). Average and worst case O(log₂ n).
  • Maximum comparisons = ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1: 10 elements → 4, 1000 elements → 10, 10 lakh elements → 20.
  • Can be written iteratively or recursively.
  • Disadvantages: the data must be sorted, and it needs direct (index) access, so it is not suitable for linked lists.

Linear searchBinary search
Data may be unsortedData must be sorted
Compares elements one by oneCompares with the middle and halves the range
Time O(n)Time O(log n)
Simple to writeSlightly more complex
Works on arrays and linked listsNeeds an array (direct access)
Good for small listsGood for large lists
1000 elements: up to 1000 comparisons1000 elements: at most 10 comparisons

h.en: 5.3.1 Hashing: Key, Hash Table and Hash Function

body.en:
Hashing is a technique that finds the storage location of a record directly from its key, using a formula, so that searching takes O(1) time on average, without comparing many elements.

Terms

  • Key: the field that uniquely identifies a record and is used to store and find it, e.g. enrolment number, employee ID.
  • Hash table: an array of fixed size m in which the records are stored. Each position is called a slot or bucket.
  • Hash function h(k): a function that converts a key k into a slot address (index) between 0 and m − 1.
  • Hash address / hash value: the index produced by the hash function.
  • Collision: when two different keys give the same hash address, e.g. 2466 % 10 = 6 and 3456 % 10 = 6.

Qualities of a good hash function

  • Easy and fast to compute.
  • Distributes keys uniformly over the table.
  • Produces as few collisions as possible.
  • Uses all parts of the key.

Applications

Symbol tables in compilers, database indexing, password storage, caches, and dictionaries (e.g. Python dict).

The key is divided by the table size m, and the remainder is the hash address:

h(k) = k mod m

  • The address lies between 0 and m − 1.
  • m should preferably be a prime number (not close to a power of 2 or 10) to spread the keys better.
  • Example: m = 97, k = 1234 → 1234 mod 97 = 70. With m = 10, k = 1234 → 4.
  • Advantage: the simplest and fastest method. Disadvantage: a bad choice of m causes many collisions.

The key is squared, and the required number of digits are taken from the middle of the result as the address:

h(k) = middle digits of k²

  • The number of digits taken depends on the table size (2 digits for a table of 100 slots, 3 for 1000).
  • Example: k = 3205 → k² = 10272025 → middle 2 digits = 72.
  • Example: k = 4567 → k² = 20857489 → middle 2 digits = 57.
  • Advantage: the middle digits depend on all digits of the key, so the distribution is good.
  • Disadvantage: squaring large keys can overflow; the same positions must be used for every key.

The key is divided into parts of equal size (the last part may be shorter), and the parts are added. The last digits of the sum (as many as the address size) form the hash address; the final carry is ignored.

1. Fold shifting

The parts are added as they are.
k = 12345678, parts of 2 digits: 12 + 34 + 56 + 78 = 180 → address 80.

2. Fold boundary

Alternate parts (the outer / boundary parts) are reversed before adding.
k = 123456789, parts of 3: 321 + 456 + 987 = 1764 → address 764.
(Fold shifting of the same key: 123 + 456 + 789 = 1368 → 368.)

  • Useful when keys are very long (phone numbers, account numbers).
  • All digits of the key take part in the address.

A collision occurs when a hash function gives the same address for two different keys. Since the table is smaller than the range of keys, collisions cannot be avoided completely; they must be handled.

1. Open addressing: linear probing

If slot h(k) is occupied, try the next slots one by one, (h(k) + 1) mod m, (h(k) + 2) mod m, …, until a free slot is found. Searching follows the same sequence. Disadvantage: clustering (keys pile up in groups).

2. Chaining (separate chaining)

Each slot holds a linked list of all keys that hash to it. A colliding key is simply added to the list (an application of linked lists).

Other methods: quadratic probing and double hashing.

expl.en:
• Adjacent elements are compared, and swapped if the left one is bigger. After pass 1 the largest value (78) is at the end.
  • The inner loop runs n − 1 − i times, because the last i elements are already in place.
  • The swapped flag stops the sort early: pass 4 makes no swap, so the array is already sorted and pass 5 is skipped.

title.en: Bubble sort: count comparisons and swaps

programs.out:
Sorted : comp =  5, swaps =  0
Reverse: comp = 15, swaps = 15
Random : comp = 14, swaps =  7

expl.en:
• Best case (already sorted): one pass, n − 1 = 5 comparisons, 0 swaps → O(n).
  • Worst case (reverse order): n(n − 1)/2 = 15 comparisons and 15 swaps → O(n²).
  • The random input needs 14 comparisons and 7 swaps.

• In pass i, the index of the smallest element of a[i..n−1] is found and that element is swapped into position i.
  • The sorted part grows from the left by one element every pass.
  • There is at most one swap per pass (n − 1 swaps in total), but the comparisons are always n(n − 1)/2 = 15, even for sorted data → O(n²) in every case.

• The left part a[0..i−1] is always sorted. The next element (key) is inserted into it.
  • Bigger elements are shifted one place right until the correct position of the key is found.
  • Best case (sorted data): no shifting, O(n). Worst case (reverse order): O(n²). It is very good for small or nearly sorted data.

title.en: Quick sort (pivot = first element) with partition trace

expl.en:
• Divide and conquer: partition() places the pivot at its final position k, with smaller values on its left and larger values on its right.
  • i moves right while a[i] ≤ pivot, j moves left while a[j] > pivot; out-of-place pairs are swapped. When i and j cross, the pivot is swapped with a[j].
  • The two parts are sorted recursively. Each output line shows one pivot reaching its final place.
  • Average O(n log n); worst case O(n²) when the data is already sorted.

• Divide: split the array at m = (l + r) / 2 until each part has one element.
  • Conquer and combine: merge() joins two sorted halves into one sorted part using a temporary array.
  • The output shows each merge: [0..1] = 27 38, then [2..3] = 3 43, then [0..3] = 3 27 38 43, and so on.
  • Always O(n log n) (best, average and worst), but it needs O(n) extra memory.

title.en: Radix sort (LSD, base 10) with pass output

expl.en:
• Numbers are put into buckets 0–9 by the units digit, collected in bucket order, then distributed again by the tens digit, then the hundreds digit.
  • The number of passes = the number of digits in the largest number (802 → 3 passes).
  • No element is compared with another. Time O(d × n), where d = number of digits.
  • Collecting in order keeps the earlier passes' order (stable), which is why it works.

programs.out:
56 at [4], comp=5
34 at [0], comp=1
99 not found

expl.en:
• Each element is compared with the key from the first to the last.
  • Best case: key at the first position (34): 1 comparison. Worst case: key at the end or not present (99): n comparisons.
  • Works on unsorted data. Time O(n).

expl.en:
• The array must be sorted.
  • Compare the key with the middle element: if equal, it is found; if smaller, search the left half (high = mid − 1); if larger, the right half (low = mid + 1).
  • Half of the remaining elements are discarded each step: 23 is found in 4 steps instead of up to 10 → O(log n).

• The same logic written recursively: each call searches one half.
  • The base case low > high means the range is empty, so the function returns −1 (not found).
  • The output gives the index of each key, or −1 for 60.

• Bubble sort works for strings too: strcmp(a, b) > 0 means a comes after b in dictionary order.
  • Strings cannot be assigned with =, so strcpy is used to swap them through a temporary array.

title.en: Hash table: division method with linear probing

expl.en:
• Hash function (division method): h(k) = k % 10 gives the slot directly, so most searches need only one comparison.
  • 3456 also hashes to 6 (already used by 2466): a collision. With linear probing the next free slot is used: 7 and 8 are full, so it goes to slot 9.
  • Searching follows the same probe sequence; −1 means not found. (−1 in the table marks an empty slot.)

• Mid-square: square the key and take the middle 2 digits: 3205² = 10272025 → 72. The middle digits depend on all digits of the key, so the spread is good.
  • Folding (shift folding): split the key into 2-digit parts from the left and add them: 12 + 34 + 56 + 78 = 180 → keep the last 2 digits → 80.
  • For 9876543 the last part has one digit: 98 + 76 + 54 + 3 = 231 → 31.

title.en: Compare bubble, selection and insertion sort (comparisons)

programs.out:
input  bubble select insert
sorted      7     28      7
reverse    28     28     28
random     27     28     19

expl.en:
• The same three inputs of 8 elements are given to each algorithm, and the comparisons are counted.
  • Sorted input: bubble (with flag) and insertion need only n − 1 = 7 comparisons (best case O(n)); selection still needs 28.
  • Reverse input: all need n(n − 1)/2 = 28 comparisons (worst case O(n²)).
  • Insertion sort usually makes the fewest comparisons on random data.

q.en: What is sorting?

a.en: Arranging data in ascending or descending order.

q.en: Internal vs external sorting?

a.en: Internal sorting works on data in main memory; external sorting is used when the data is on disk because it is too large for memory.

q.en: What is a stable sort?

a.en: A sort that keeps equal elements in their original relative order, e.g. bubble, insertion, merge.

q.en: How does bubble sort work?

a.en: It repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are out of order; the largest element moves to the end in each pass.

q.en: What is the best case of bubble sort?

a.en: O(n), when the array is already sorted and a swap flag is used.

q.en: How does selection sort work?

a.en: In each pass it selects the smallest element of the unsorted part and swaps it with the first unsorted position.

q.en: Which simple sort makes the fewest swaps?

a.en: Selection sort: at most n − 1 swaps.

q.en: How does insertion sort work?

a.en: Each element is inserted into its correct place in the sorted left part by shifting larger elements right.

q.en: When is insertion sort best?

a.en: For small or nearly sorted data: O(n) in the best case.

q.en: What is a pivot in quick sort?

a.en: The element around which the array is partitioned; after partitioning it is at its final position.

q.en: Worst case of quick sort and when?

a.en: O(n²), when the array is already sorted and the first element is the pivot.

q.en: What is the principle of quick sort and merge sort?

a.en: Divide and conquer.

q.en: Time complexity of merge sort?

a.en: O(n log n) in all cases; it needs O(n) extra space.

q.en: How many passes does radix sort need?

a.en: Equal to the number of digits in the largest number.

q.en: Which sort does not compare elements?

a.en: Radix sort.

q.en: What is linear search?

a.en: Comparing the key with every element one by one until it is found or the list ends.

q.en: Time complexity of linear search?

a.en: O(n); best case O(1).

q.en: What is the condition for binary search?

a.en: The data must be sorted and directly accessible (array).

q.en: How is mid calculated in binary search?

a.en: mid = (low + high) / 2.

q.en: Time complexity of binary search?

a.en: O(log n).

q.en: Maximum comparisons in binary search of 1000 elements?
What is hashing?

a.en: A technique that computes the storage address of a record directly from its key using a hash function.

q.en: What is a hash table?

a.en: An array of slots in which records are stored at addresses given by the hash function.

q.en: What is a hash function?

a.en: A function that converts a key into a table index.

q.en: Explain the division method.

a.en: h(k) = k mod m, where m is the table size (preferably prime).

q.en: Explain the mid-square method.

a.en: Square the key and take the middle digits as the address.

q.en: Explain the folding method.

a.en: Split the key into parts, add them, and take the last digits of the sum as the address.

q.en: What is a collision?

a.en: When two different keys produce the same hash address.

q.en: Name two collision resolution methods.

a.en: Linear probing (open addressing) and chaining.
